docs.title: Stepper-C — stepper motor control from model to metal
docs.text: Quick start

docs.title: A driver instance, two loops, four callbacks
docs.text:
Stepper-C needs two functions from your board — one that writes the PWM compare values and one that switches the gate drivers on or off — and two periodic calls: the fast loop in the PWM/ADC interrupt and the slow loop at 1 kHz.

#include "sstep.h"

/* Board functions (your HAL) */
extern void board_pwm_set(const uint16_t compare[SSTEP_LEGS_MAX]);
extern void board_gate_enable(bool on);

static int pwm_write(void* ctx, const uint16_t cmp[SSTEP_LEGS_MAX])
{
    (void)ctx;
    board_pwm_set(cmp);
    return 0;
}

static int output_enable(void* ctx, bool on)
{
    (void)ctx;
    board_gate_enable(on);
    return 0;
}

static struct sstep motor;

void app_start(const struct sstep_config* cfg)   /* cfg.hal uses the two functions */
{
    (void)sstep_init(&motor, cfg);
    (void)sstep_enable(&motor);
    (void)sstep_move_to(&motor, 3200);           /* one revolution at 1/16 */
}

void adc_isr(uint16_t ia, uint16_t ib, uint16_t vbus)   /* 20 kHz */
{
    const struct sstep_sample s = { ia, ib, vbus };
    (void)sstep_fast_loop(&motor, &s);
}

void tick_1khz(void)
{
    (void)sstep_slow_loop(&motor);
}

A complete configuration for the 17HS19-2004S1 motor on the B-G431B-ESC1 board is in Using the library. Before the first motor turns on the bench, run the same code in the software-in-the-loop diagram.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: The public API of Stepper-C 0.1.0 is declared in inc/sstep_ctrl.h and included through sstep.h. All functions return an int status code, never block and never allocate. Types and members marked private may change in any release.

docs.title: Headers
docs.text: Header Content sstep.h umbrella header and version (SSTEP_VERSION, fallback "0.1.0") inc/sstep_config.h build-time macros (see Build-time configuration) inc/sstep_defs.h status codes, enum sstep_topology, fault flags, enum sstep_state inc/sstep_math.h numeric types (sstep_real_t, sstep_acc_t, sstep_angle_t, struct sstep_gain) inc/sstep_ctrl.h configuration, callbacks, loops, commands

docs.title: Status codes
docs.text: Code Value Meaning SSTEP_OK 0 success SSTEP_ERR_PARAM −1 NULL pointer, missing required callback, value out of range SSTEP_ERR_CONFIG −2 values that are valid alone but inconsistent together SSTEP_ERR_STATE −3 command not allowed in the current state (disabled, faulted, moving) SSTEP_ERR_UNSUPPORTED −4 topology not compiled in

docs.title: Enumerations and flags
docs.text: Name Values enum sstep_topology SSTEP_TOPOLOGY_FULL_BRIDGE = 0 (4 legs), SSTEP_TOPOLOGY_SHARED_LEG = 1 (3 legs); SSTEP_LEGS_MAX = 4 enum sstep_drive_mode SSTEP_DRIVE_CURRENT = 0 (PI current control), SSTEP_DRIVE_VOLTAGE = 1 (open loop R·I + ff) enum sstep_state SSTEP_STATE_DISABLED = 0, SSTEP_STATE_HOLDING = 1, SSTEP_STATE_MOVING = 2, SSTEP_STATE_FAULT = 3 enum sstep_event SSTEP_EVENT_MOVE_DONE = 0, SSTEP_EVENT_HOLD_CURRENT = 1 Fault flags (uint16_t) SSTEP_FAULT_NONE 0x0000, …_OVERCURRENT 0x0001, …_OVERVOLTAGE 0x0002, …_UNDERVOLTAGE 0x0004, …_HAL 0x0008, …_EXTERNAL 0x0010

docs.title: Callbacks
docs.text:
typedef int  (*sstep_pwm_write_fn)(void* context, const uint16_t compare[SSTEP_LEGS_MAX]);
typedef int  (*sstep_output_enable_fn)(void* context, bool enable);
typedef void (*sstep_fault_fn)(void* context, uint16_t faults);
typedef void (*sstep_event_fn)(void* context, enum sstep_event event);
Callback Required Called from Contract pwm_write yes fast loop (interrupt) write one compare value per leg (0 … pwm_period_ticks; 0 = low side on); the array is valid only during the call; return < 0 on error (raises SSTEP_FAULT_HAL) output_enable yes enable, disable, any fault true enables the gate drivers, false switches every leg off (high impedance); return < 0 on error on_fault no the context that detected the fault (may be the interrupt) newly raised flags on_event no slow loop move done, hold current applied

docs.title: struct sstep (private)
docs.text: The driver instance, allocated by the application and initialised by sstep_init(). Its members (configuration copy, derived gains, double-buffered setpoint, PI integrators, motion state, faults, state) are private; use the functions only.

docs.title: sstep_init()
docs.text:
int sstep_init(struct sstep* m, const struct sstep_config* cfg);

Validates the configuration, copies it, derives the per-unit gains (Kp = L ωc, Ki = R ωc, Kb = Ts R / L), the ADC scaling, the trip levels and the motion limits. No floating point is used with the fixed point backend. The outputs stay disabled.

Parameter Meaning m driver instance cfg configuration; copied Returns When SSTEP_OK state SSTEP_STATE_DISABLED SSTEP_ERR_PARAM NULL pointer, missing pwm_write/output_enable, a field out of range SSTEP_ERR_CONFIG inconsistent fields (trip above full scale, run current above trip or rated, loop rates, bandwidth, bus thresholds, gains that do not fit) SSTEP_ERR_UNSUPPORTED topology not compiled in

docs.title: sstep_enable()
docs.text:
int sstep_enable(struct sstep* m);

Enables the outputs and holds the current position with the run current (the hold current follows after hold_delay_ms). Resets the integrators. No effect when already enabled.

Returns When SSTEP_OK state SSTEP_STATE_HOLDING SSTEP_ERR_PARAM m is NULL SSTEP_ERR_STATE faulted, or output_enable() failed (then SSTEP_FAULT_HAL)

docs.title: sstep_disable()
docs.text:
int sstep_disable(struct sstep* m);

Stops immediately and switches the outputs off: the motor coasts without holding torque. A faulted driver stays faulted. Returns SSTEP_OK or SSTEP_ERR_PARAM.

docs.title: sstep_fast_loop()
docs.text:
int sstep_fast_loop(struct sstep* m, const struct sstep_sample* sample);

Call once per PWM period from the PWM/ADC interrupt. Converts the sample, checks the overcurrent and bus voltage trips (when the outputs are on), runs the current controllers, limits and maps the voltage and calls pwm_write(). Bounded execution time. With the outputs off it only stores the measurements.

Returns When SSTEP_OK always, except: SSTEP_ERR_PARAM NULL pointer (only with SSTEP_CFG_ARG_CHECKS = 1)

docs.title: sstep_slow_loop()
docs.text:
int sstep_slow_loop(struct sstep* m);

Call at slow_loop_hz. Advances the motion generator, selects run or hold current, updates the bus voltage scale, publishes the setpoint for the fast loop, sets the state (HOLDING/MOVING, or FAULT if the fast loop tripped meanwhile) and reports events. Returns SSTEP_OK or SSTEP_ERR_PARAM.

docs.title: sstep_move_to(), sstep_move_by()
docs.text:
int sstep_move_to(struct sstep* m, int32_t position);
int sstep_move_by(struct sstep* m, int32_t delta);

Start a move to an absolute position, or relative to the current target, with the trapezoidal profile. A running command is replaced smoothly (no velocity step).

Returns When SSTEP_OK move started SSTEP_ERR_PARAM m is NULL; move_by target outside int32_t SSTEP_ERR_STATE disabled or faulted

docs.title: sstep_run()
docs.text:
int sstep_run(struct sstep* m, int32_t velocity);

Run at a constant signed velocity [µsteps/s] until another command, accelerating with the configured limits. |velocity| ≤ v_max. Returns SSTEP_OK, SSTEP_ERR_PARAM (NULL or velocity above v_max) or SSTEP_ERR_STATE (disabled or faulted).

docs.title: sstep_stop()
docs.text:
int sstep_stop(struct sstep* m);

Decelerates to standstill with the deceleration limit, then holds. No effect when nothing moves. Returns SSTEP_OK or SSTEP_ERR_PARAM.

docs.title: sstep_set_position()
docs.text:
int sstep_set_position(struct sstep* m, int32_t position);

Redefines the current position (homing). The rotor does not move: the electrical angle is kept and only the numbering changes. Returns SSTEP_OK, SSTEP_ERR_PARAM or SSTEP_ERR_STATE (a command is running).

docs.title: sstep_set_current()
docs.text:
int sstep_set_current(struct sstep* m, uint32_t run_ma, uint32_t hold_ma);

Changes the run and hold currents; used from the next slow loop period.

Returns When SSTEP_OK accepted SSTEP_ERR_PARAM NULL, run_ma = 0, a value above 10⁷ SSTEP_ERR_CONFIG hold_ma > run_ma, run_ma above i_trip_ma or i_rated_ma

docs.title: sstep_set_motion_limits()
docs.text:
int sstep_set_motion_limits(struct sstep* m, uint32_t v_max, uint32_t accel, uint32_t decel);

Changes the velocity [µsteps/s], acceleration and deceleration [µsteps/s²] limits (decel = 0: same as accel). The motion generator uses them from the next slow loop period, also for a running move. Returns SSTEP_ERR_PARAM for zero values or values that become zero or too large in the internal units (for example an acceleration below slow_loop_hz² / 65536).

docs.title: sstep_report_fault()
docs.text:
int sstep_report_fault(struct sstep* m, uint16_t faults);

Raises application faults (a driver fault pin, over-temperature), typically SSTEP_FAULT_EXTERNAL: the outputs switch off and the state becomes FAULT. May be called from an interrupt. Returns SSTEP_OK or SSTEP_ERR_PARAM.

docs.title: sstep_clear_faults()
docs.text:
int sstep_clear_faults(struct sstep* m);

Clears all faults; the driver goes to DISABLED and must be enabled again. Returns SSTEP_OK or SSTEP_ERR_PARAM.

docs.title: sstep_get_status()
docs.text:
int sstep_get_status(const struct sstep* m, struct sstep_status* status);

Fills a snapshot in engineering units (state, faults, position, target, velocity, currents, bus voltage). Returns SSTEP_OK or SSTEP_ERR_PARAM.

docs.title: Control Algorithms
docs.text: This chapter explains every algorithm of Stepper-C: the timing of the two loops, the number formats, the current controller, the mapping of the voltage to the power stage legs, the motion generator and the fault handling. The same algorithms are implemented in the Scilab prototype (model/) and in the Python twins (tools/); where the prototype differs, it says so.

docs.title: Two loops and the hand-off
docs.text:
Loop Rate (default) Context Work Fast fast_loop_hz = 20 kHz (PWM frequency) PWM / ADC interrupt ADC conversion, trips, current references, PI, feed-forward, voltage limit, leg mapping, pwm_write() Slow slow_loop_hz = 1 kHz main loop or timer task motion generator, run/hold current, bus voltage scale, setpoint, events

fast_loop_hz must be an integer multiple of slow_loop_hz; the ratio (20 by default) is stored as ratio.

Hand-off. The slow loop writes a complete setpoint — electrical angle at the start of its period, angle increment per fast period, current amplitude, back-EMF feed-forward, bus voltage scale — into the buffer the fast loop is not using, then sets sp_pending. The fast loop swaps buffers at its next tick. On a single-core MCU this needs no lock: the fast loop never reads the buffer being written, and the flag is cleared before writing.

Angle interpolation. Between hand-offs the fast loop adds the increment Δ to the angle every tick, at most ratio times; if the slow loop is late, the angle stops instead of running ahead.

docs.title: Numbers: per unit, fixed point and float
docs.text:
All signals inside the loops are per unit:

Quantity Base 1.0 pu means Current i_full_scale_ma (ADC full scale) the current at the end of the ADC range Voltage vbus_nominal_mv the nominal bus voltage Angle 2³² one electrical turn Type Fixed point backend Float backend Signal sstep_real_t Q15 in int16_t (−1 … 1) float Accumulator sstep_acc_t Q15 in int32_t (±65536 pu) float PI integrator sstep_integ_t Q27 in int32_t (keeps increments far below one LSB of Q15) float Gain struct sstep_gain Q15 mantissa + shift exponent float Angle sstep_angle_t uint32_t, wraps at one turn same

Every operation saturates instead of wrapping, in both backends with identical ranges. sstep_init() derives all gains from the integer configuration without floating point (2π is taken as 710/113, error 8.5·10⁻⁸). The sine and cosine come from a quarter-wave table (SSTEP_CFG_SINE_TABLE_BITS = 8: 257 entries) with linear interpolation; the measured error is 1.0 LSB (3.05·10⁻⁵) in fixed point and 4.7·10⁻⁶ in float.

Microstep angle. One microstep is 2³⁰ / M of an electrical turn (four full steps per turn). The electrical angle of a position is pos << (14 − log₂ M) with the position in 1/65536 microstep; positions therefore wrap exactly at one electrical turn.

docs.title: Current references
docs.text:
From the angle \(\varphi\) and the amplitude \(I\) of the setpoint:

\[ i_A^* = I \cos\varphi, \qquad i_B^* = I \sin\varphi \]

The amplitude is i_run_ma while the motor moves and i_hold_ma after hold_delay_ms of standstill (event SSTEP_EVENT_HOLD_CURRENT). sstep_enable() starts with the run current.

docs.title: Current controller
docs.text:
One PI controller per phase, the same for both:

\[ \begin{aligned} e_k &= i_k^* - i_k \\ v_k^* &= K_p\,e_k + \mathrm{integ}_k + v_{\mathrm{ff},k} \\ \mathrm{integ}_k &\leftarrow \mathrm{integ}_k + K_i T_s\,e_k + K_b\,\left(v_{k,\mathrm{applied}} - v_k^*\right) \end{aligned} \]

with \(k \in \{A, B\}\), the integrator state \(\mathrm{integ}_k\) and the back-EMF feed-forward \(v_{\mathrm{ff},k}\); the \(K_b\) term acts only while the voltage is limited.

Gain Formula 17HS19-2004S1, 1 kHz \(K_p\) \(L\,\omega_c\) 18.85 V/A \(K_i\) \(R\,\omega_c\) 10 053 V/(A·s) \(K_b\) (back-calculation) \(T_s R / L\) (tracking time \(L/R\)) 0.0267 per period

Pole-zero cancellation. The PI zero \(K_i/K_p = R/L\) cancels the pole of the R-L phase, so the closed current loop is first order with the bandwidth \(\omega_c = 2\pi \cdot\) current_bw_hz (1 kHz by default; current_bw_hz must not exceed fast_loop_hz / 4). The computation delay of one PWM period (the voltage computed now is applied in the next period) adds a small overshoot: the measured step 0 → 2 A has 1.12 % overshoot, 0.35 ms rise time (90 %) and 0.40 ms settling time (2 %) with both topologies (test T04).

Anti-windup. When the power stage cannot produce the requested voltage, the difference between the applied and the requested voltage pulls the integrator back with the gain \(K_b\) (back-calculation). The integrator does not wind up during acceleration into the voltage limit, and the current recovers without overshoot when the limit ends.

Back-EMF feed-forward. From the commanded speed (the position change of the slow period), the slow loop computes the back-EMF amplitude \(K_t\,\omega\) and the fast loop adds

\[ v_{\mathrm{ff},A} = -K_t\,\omega \sin\varphi, \qquad v_{\mathrm{ff},B} = K_t\,\omega \cos\varphi \]

to the controller outputs. The PI then only corrects the residual. With ke_uv_s_per_rad = 0 the feed-forward is off.

Voltage drive. With drive_mode = SSTEP_DRIVE_VOLTAGE there is no current measurement: \(v_k^* = R\,i_k^* + v_{\mathrm{ff},k}\). Torque then drops with speed (the inductance is not compensated); use it only for boards without current sensing.

Known limitation: phase lag at speed

The loop follows a rotating reference with a lag that grows with the electrical frequency (about 4° at 1 rev/s; at 4 rev/s the current vector error is 0.41 A rms). The amplitude stays close to the reference up to the voltage limit (1.97 A at 4 rev/s), but the lag shifts the torque angle. A delay compensation (angle advance by one period) is planned; an inductive feed-forward \(L\,di/dt\) was tried in the prototype and made the result worse.

docs.title: Voltage limit and leg mapping
docs.text:
The requested phase voltages (v_A, v_B) are divided by the measured bus voltage (a = v_A / Vbus, b = v_B / Vbus) and mapped to leg duty cycles:

Topology Feasible when Leg duties Largest circular amplitude Two H-bridges, legs [A+ A− B+ B−] max(|a|, |b|) ≤ 1 0.5 + a/2, 0.5 − a/2, 0.5 + b/2, 0.5 − b/2 Vbus Shared leg, legs [U V W], A = U − W, B = V − W max(a, b, 0) − min(a, b, 0) ≤ 1 a + w, b + w, w with w = 0.5 − (max + min)/2 Vbus / √2

When the request is not feasible, both components are scaled by the same factor: the voltage vector keeps its direction, so the current — and the torque — keeps its angle; only its magnitude is limited. The limited flag switches the anti-windup on.

Implementation details: the request is first halved (exact power-of-two pre-scale) until it is below 4 pu, then multiplied by V_base / Vbus (computed once per slow period from the bus voltage ADC), and a division happens only when the request is limited. The common leg of the shared topology is centred between the highest and the lowest leg voltage, which gives the largest circular amplitude. Duties become compare values 0 … pwm_period_ticks (0 = low side on).

docs.title: Motion generator
docs.text:
The motion generator runs in the slow loop and uses integers only in both numeric backends:

Quantity Unit Position pos, target 1/65536 microstep (int64_t) Velocity vel, v_max 1/65536 microstep per slow period (int32_t, below 2³⁰) Acceleration acc, deceleration dec 1/65536 microstep per period²

Every period:

  1. Target velocity. In RUN mode, the requested velocity limited to v_max. In MOVE mode, the largest velocity v_new for which the distance of this period \((v + v_{\mathrm{new}})/2\) plus the braking distance \(v_{\mathrm{new}}^2 / (2\,\mathrm{dec})\) still fits into the distance left rem:

    \[ v_{\mathrm{new}} = \frac{-d + \sqrt{d^2 + 8\,d\,|r| - 4\,d\,|v|}}{2} \]

    with \(d\) = dec, \(r\) = rem

    (integer square root), or v_max when the distance left is larger than the braking distance from v_max plus one period. 2. Rate limit. The velocity moves towards the target by at most acc when speeding up (larger magnitude, same direction) and at most dec otherwise. 3. Integration. pos += floor((v + v_new) / 2) (trapezoidal rule). 4. End of a move. When the position crosses the target, or comes within 64/65536 microstep of it with |v_new| ≤ dec, the position snaps to the target, the velocity to zero, the mode to HOLD and SSTEP_EVENT_MOVE_DONE is reported.

Properties, all covered by unit tests: no overshoot; the move ends exactly on the target; the velocity never changes by more than acc or dec in a period, except in the last period of a move where at most 2·dec (a few microsteps per second) drops to zero; a new target while moving changes the profile smoothly (decelerating with dec if it lies behind). A move of 6400 microsteps with 16 000 µsteps/s and 160 000 µsteps/s² takes 499 periods (T05). The Scilab and Python implementations are bit-exact copies.

The electrical angle increment for the fast loop is Δ = trunc(Δpos · 2^(14 − log₂ M) / ratio), re-synchronised at every hand-off.

docs.title: States and faults
docs.text:
State Outputs Entered by SSTEP_STATE_DISABLED off (all legs high impedance) sstep_init(), sstep_disable(), sstep_clear_faults() SSTEP_STATE_HOLDING on, position held sstep_enable(); slow loop when a command ends SSTEP_STATE_MOVING on, command running slow loop while a move, run or stop executes SSTEP_STATE_FAULT off a trip in the fast loop, a callback error, sstep_report_fault() Fault flag Raised when Where SSTEP_FAULT_OVERCURRENT (0x0001) |i_a| or |i_b| above i_trip_ma (current drive only) fast loop, same period SSTEP_FAULT_OVERVOLTAGE (0x0002) bus voltage above vbus_max_mv fast loop SSTEP_FAULT_UNDERVOLTAGE (0x0004) bus voltage below vbus_min_mv fast loop SSTEP_FAULT_HAL (0x0008) pwm_write() or output_enable() returned an error any SSTEP_FAULT_EXTERNAL (0x0010) the application reported a fault sstep_report_fault()

On a fault the outputs are switched off immediately (output_enable(false)), the flags are stored and on_fault() is called from the context that detected it — possibly the interrupt. Faults stay active until sstep_clear_faults(); the driver then returns to DISABLED and must be enabled again.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This chapter installs the tools, gets the three repositories and runs each part once: the library tests, the simulation tests, the software-in-the-loop diagram and the ngspice model. Each section can be done on its own; the order below is the one that needs the fewest tools first.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Tool Version Needed for Notes Git any all CMake 3.21+ library presets need 3.21 C compiler GCC 11+, Clang 14+ or MSVC 2022 library, SIL the SIL build uses the compiler Scilab finds Python 3.9+ twins, ngspice runner, docs numpy, scipy, matplotlib Scilab 2027.0.0 (2025 and 2026 work) simulation, SIL includes Xcos Visual Studio 2022 or Build Tools "Desktop development with C++" SIL on Windows Scilab compiles the Xcos blocks with it ngspice 42+ (tested 45.2) power stage model console executable GoogleTest, gcov from the presets library unit tests fetched by CMake

Get the repositories into one folder:

mkdir sfs-stepper && cd sfs-stepper
git clone https://github.com/AntonVynohradov/Stepper-C.git sfs-stepper-ctrl
git clone https://github.com/AntonVynohradov/sfs-stepper-sim.git
git clone https://github.com/AntonVynohradov/sfs-stepper-power-spice.git

The library repository Stepper-C is cloned into the folder sfs-stepper-ctrl: the simulation looks for the library under that name (or in SSTEP_CTRL_DIR).

docs.title: Library: build and test
docs.text:
The library uses CMake presets. The preset names carry the configuration in brackets:

Preset What it builds [Debug]Stepper Motor Control static library, debug [Release]Stepper Motor Control static library, optimised [UnitTests]Stepper Motor Control GoogleTest suite, fixed point backend, coverage [UnitTestsFloat]Stepper Motor Control GoogleTest suite, float backend [IntegrationTests]Stepper Motor Control pytest integration tests (placeholder) [Examples]Stepper Motor Control host examples (placeholder) 
cd sfs-stepper-ctrl
cmake --preset "[UnitTests]Stepper Motor Control"
cmake --build "build/[UnitTests]Stepper Motor Control"
ctest --test-dir "build/[UnitTests]Stepper Motor Control" --output-on-failure

Expected result: 76 tests pass (75 with the float preset). VS Code users find the same steps as tasks (Terminal → Run Task).

docs.title: Simulation: run the tests
docs.text:
1. Open Scilab and change to the sfs-stepper-sim folder.
  2. Run the test runner:
exec("tests/run_all.sce", -1);

or from a terminal (exit status 1 on a failure, for CI):

scilab-cli -f tests/run_all.sce

Each test prints one line PASS name: measured values or FAIL …, and the runner ends with the number of failures. The full run takes a few minutes; T10 (switching stage) and T11 (resonance sweep) take the longest.

The Python twins run without Scilab:

cd sfs-stepper-sim
python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
python tools/ref_model.py        # T00–T02, motor model
python tools/ref_ctrl.py         # B01, T03, T04, current loop
python tools/ref_motion.py       # T05–T07, T09, motion generator
python tools/ref_switching.py    # T10, switching stage
python tools/ref_ext.py          # T08, T11, T12

docs.title: Software in the loop: see the motor turn
docs.text:
1. Make sure sfs-stepper-ctrl is next to sfs-stepper-sim (or set SSTEP_CTRL_DIR).
  2. Open start_sil.sce in Scilab and press F5. The first time, Scilab compiles the library and the Xcos blocks (a few seconds); later it only links them, and it rebuilds automatically when a source file changed.
  3. Xcos opens xcos/stepper_sil.zcos. Press Start (▶).

The scope shows the phase currents with their references, the speed, the load angle and the commanded and real rotor positions. The scenario is edited in Simulation → Set Context; see Software in the Loop for every variable.

After an update of the blocks

When the block interface changed (new outputs, parameters), set sil_regenerate = %t in start_sil.sce once, or delete xcos/stepper_sil.zcos; the diagram is generated again from xcos/sil_diagram.sci. Restart Scilab when the library was rebuilt, because Windows keeps the old DLL loaded.

docs.title: Power stage: run ngspice
docs.text:
1. Install ngspice. On Windows, download the 64-bit zip from https://ngspice.sourceforge.io/download.html, unpack it and point NGSPICE to Spice64\bin\ngspice_con.exe (or install mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-ngspice in MSYS2). On Linux, apt install ngspice.
  2. Run the tests and export the parameters to the simulation:
cd sfs-stepper-power-spice
python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
python tools/run_tests.py --export     # about 40 s
python tools/plot_leg.py               # docs/leg_edges.png

The runner prints SP01–SP03 and writes export/stage_esc1.json and, when ../sfs-stepper-sim exists, params/stage_esc1_spice.sci and .json there.

docs.title: This manual
docs.text:
The manual is built from Markdown with MkDocs Material (website) and WeasyPrint (PDF):

git clone https://github.com/SystemFromScratch-Articles/Stepper-C-Motor-Control-Library.git sfs-stepper-article
cd sfs-stepper-article
python -m pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
mkdocs serve                              # http://127.0.0.1:8000

WeasyPrint needs the Pango library: on Windows install mingw-w64-x86_64-pango in MSYS2 (the build script finds C:\msys64\mingw64\bin by itself), on Linux apt install libpango-1.0-0 libpangoft2-1.0-0.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Anti-windup (back-calculation) Feedback of the difference between the applied and the requested voltage into the PI integrator while the power stage limits the voltage, so the integrator does not grow without bound. Back-EMF The voltage induced in a phase by the moving rotor, K_t ω in amplitude. Bootstrap The supply of the high-side gate driver: a capacitor charged from VCC through a diode (in the L6387E a DMOS) while the low side conducts. Centre-aligned PWM PWM whose counter counts up and down; the pulses of all legs are centred in the period, and the counter peak is a common instant at which all low sides conduct. Dead time The interval in which both transistors of a leg are off, inserted to prevent a short circuit. The timer dead time is programmed; the effective dead time is its net effect on the phase voltage after the driver and transistor delays. Detent torque The torque of the permanent magnet on the unpowered motor, periodic with one full step. Electrical angle p θ: one electrical turn equals four full steps. Feed-forward A control signal computed from a model (here the back-EMF from the commanded speed) and added to the controller output. Hold current The reduced phase current applied after a standstill time, to limit heating. Leg A half-bridge: two transistors in series between the bus and ground, with the output between them. Load angle δ = φ − p θ, the electrical angle between the current vector and the rotor. Mid-band instability A rotor oscillation that appears at medium speeds when the drive cannot control the current any more (voltage limit) and the back-EMF coupling undamps the rotor. Miller plateau The gate voltage at which a MOSFET switches; the gate current then only charges the gate-drain capacitance while the drain voltage changes. Per unit (pu) A quantity divided by its base value (current: ADC full scale; voltage: nominal bus voltage). Pole-zero cancellation Choosing the PI zero at the pole of the R-L phase (Ki / Kp = R / L), so the closed loop is first order. Q15, Q27 Fixed point formats with 15 or 27 fractional bits. Shoot-through Both transistors of a leg conducting at the same time; a short circuit of the bus. SIL Software in the loop: the target code running in a simulation. Slow loop, fast loop The two periodic functions of the library: motion at 1 kHz, current control at the PWM rate. Synchronism The rotor following the rotating field; lost when the load angle exceeds about 180°. Twin An independent implementation of the same algorithm used for cross-checking. VDMOS The ngspice model of a vertical power MOSFET with body diode and non-linear capacitances.

docs.title: Hardware Bring-up
docs.text:
The next step of the project (P3) ports Stepper-C to the B-G431B-ESC1 and runs the 17HS19-2004S1. This chapter is the plan and the checklist for that step: how to connect the motor, what to measure first and how to compare the hardware with the models. It describes work that has not been done yet; results will be added in the next edition.

Safety

A two-phase motor on a three-phase board is a non-standard connection; a wrong firmware setting can short a leg. Use a laboratory supply with a current limit (start at 1 A), keep a hand on its output switch, and never connect a battery before the current loop is verified.

docs.title: Connection
docs.text:
ESC1 output Motor wire Phase U A+ phase A between U and W V B+ phase B between V and W W A− and B− joined common leg

Identify the two coils of the motor with an ohmmeter (1.6 Ω within a pair, open between pairs). The polarity of a coil only changes the direction of rotation; swapping the phases A and B reverses it too.

The common wire W carries −(i_A + i_B), up to √2 times the phase current amplitude (2.83 A at 2 A); the ESC1 leg and its shunt handle it easily.

docs.title: Measurements before the first run
docs.text:
Quantity Method Enters Phase resistance R 4-wire measurement, or a DC current from the supply and a voltmeter, at room temperature r_mohm, mot.R Phase inductance L LCR meter at 1 kHz; or the current rise time L/R with a voltage step l_uh, mot.L Back-EMF constant K_t spin the unpowered shaft with a drill, measure the open-circuit phase voltage amplitude and the speed: K_t = E/ω ke_uv_s_per_rad, mot.Kt Detent torque torque gauge or a lever and a scale on the unpowered shaft mot.Td Current sense outputs off: ADC zero of both phases; known DC current: counts per ampere adc_i_zero, adc_i_span, i_full_scale_ma Bus voltage sense ADC reading at a known supply voltage adc_vbus_mv_full Timer dead time the value programmed in the timer break/dead-time register ngspice BOARD["dead_ns"] Gate resistors, shunt value schematic MB1419 ngspice BOARD

Enter the measured values into the simulation first and rerun T01–T05: the SIL diagram then predicts what the hardware should do.

docs.title: Firmware configuration (STM32G431)
docs.text:
Item Setting PWM advanced timer, centre-aligned, 20 kHz: with a 170 MHz timer clock the auto-reload is 4250 (pwm_period_ticks) Dead time the timer's dead-time generator (start with 500 ns, the value of the models) Outputs complementary outputs of the three legs; break input for a hardware trip ADC injected conversions of the two phase shunts used by A and B and of the bus voltage, triggered at the counter peak (all low sides on) Interrupt ADC end of injected conversion → sstep_fast_loop() Slow loop 1 kHz timer or SysTick → sstep_slow_loop() Backend SSTEP_CFG_MATH_BACKEND_FLOAT (the Cortex-M4F has an FPU), shared leg only

Phase A is measured on the U shunt and phase B on the V shunt; the W shunt (common leg) can be used as a plausibility check: i_W = −(i_A + i_B).

docs.title: First power-up sequence
docs.text:
1. Outputs disabled: check the ADC zero readings and the bus voltage reading.
  2. sstep_enable() with i_run_ma = 500, locked shaft: the rotor snaps to a full step and holds. Measure the phase currents with a current probe; they must match the reference within the current sense resolution.
  3. Current step test as in T04 (enable, move by one microstep): compare overshoot and settling with the SIL run of the same configuration.
  4. Slow move (0.5 rev/s): the rotor follows; listen for the low-speed resonance around 1.2 rev/s.
  5. Raise the speed in steps up to 6 rev/s; log the current amplitude and compare with Results.
  6. Measure the execution time of sstep_fast_loop() (GPIO toggle or cycle counter).

docs.title: What to compare with the models
docs.text:
Hardware measurement Model counterpart Test Current step response prototype / SIL T04, S01 Current amplitude vs. speed prototype T09, voltage limit table Resonant speed detent resonance T11b Switch node edges, gate voltages ngspice SP02 Phase voltage error near the zero crossing switching stage T10

Differences beyond the tolerances point to a wrong parameter (most often K_t, the ADC scaling or the dead time) and are fed back into the models.

docs.title: Stepper-C Library
docs.text: Stepper-C (github.com/AntonVynohradov/Stepper-C, local folder sfs-stepper-ctrl) is the control library of the system: C11, no heap, no RTOS, no global state, two numeric backends and two power stage topologies. This chapter explains how to add it to a firmware project, configure it for a motor and a board, call its loops from the interrupts and check that it works. The functions are listed in the API Reference; the algorithms are explained in Control Algorithms.

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text: Path Content sstep.h umbrella header: include only this inc/sstep_config.h build-time configuration macros inc/sstep_defs.h status codes, topologies, fault flags, states inc/sstep_math.h numeric backend: types, saturating inline operations inc/sstep_ctrl.h the API: configuration, callbacks, loops, commands src/sstep_ctrl.c initialisation, loops, commands src/sstep_bridge.c voltage limit and leg mapping src/sstep_motion.c motion generator src/sstep_math.c, src/sstep_sin_table.c sine/cosine, gain conversions (table generated by tools/sstep_gen_sin_table.py) sstep.cmake, CMakeLists.txt, CMakePresets.json build tests/unit/ GoogleTest suites with a motor model (sstep_test_plant.hpp) tests/compile/sstep_api_check.c compile check of the API with the reference configuration

docs.title: Adding the library to a project
docs.text:
With CMake (the library is a subdirectory or a submodule):

set(SSTEP_MATH_BACKEND "FLOAT" CACHE STRING "" FORCE)   # STM32G4 has an FPU
add_subdirectory(ext/sfs-stepper-ctrl)
target_link_libraries(firmware PRIVATE sstep)
CMake variable Values Effect SSTEP_MATH_BACKEND FIXED (default), FLOAT defines SSTEP_CFG_MATH_BACKEND SSTEP_CONFIG_DIR folder adds the folder to the include path and defines SSTEP_USER_CONFIG, so sstep_user_config.h is used SSTEP_UNIT_TESTS, SSTEP_INTEGRATION_TESTS, SSTEP_EXAMPLES ON/OFF test and example targets

Without CMake: compile the five files of src/, add the repository root and inc/ to the include path, and define SSTEP_CFG_MATH_BACKEND=SSTEP_MATH_BACKEND_FLOAT (or leave it for fixed point). The library needs only <stdint.h>, <stdbool.h> and <stddef.h>.

docs.title: Build-time configuration
docs.text:
Macro Default Range Effect SSTEP_CFG_MATH_BACKEND SSTEP_MATH_BACKEND_FIXED …_FIXED, …_FLOAT Q15/Q31 integer arithmetic or single-precision float SSTEP_CFG_TOPOLOGY_FULL_BRIDGE 1 0, 1 compile support for two H-bridges SSTEP_CFG_TOPOLOGY_SHARED_LEG 1 0, 1 compile support for three legs with a shared leg SSTEP_CFG_MICROSTEPS_MAX 256 power of two 1 … 256 largest accepted microsteps SSTEP_CFG_SINE_TABLE_BITS 8 6 … 10 quarter-wave table size 2^bits + 1 (flash) SSTEP_CFG_ARG_CHECKS 1 0, 1 0 removes the pointer checks from sstep_fast_loop() only

Every macro is range-checked with #error. Set them on the compiler command line or in sstep_user_config.h:

/* sstep_user_config.h: Stepper-C for an STM32G431 driving one ESC1 */
#define SSTEP_CFG_MATH_BACKEND SSTEP_MATH_BACKEND_FLOAT
#define SSTEP_CFG_TOPOLOGY_FULL_BRIDGE 0     /* only the shared leg is needed */
#define SSTEP_CFG_MICROSTEPS_MAX 64U

Which backend? Use FIXED on cores without a hardware FPU (Cortex-M0/M0+/M3, RISC-V RV32IMC); use FLOAT where single-precision float is in hardware (Cortex-M4F/M7/M33F, STM32G4). Both give the same control behaviour within the resolution of Q15 (the closed loop tests pass with the same limits in both).

docs.title: Configuring a driver
docs.text:
The run-time configuration is one structure in integer engineering units, copied by sstep_init(). This is the reference configuration of the 17HS19-2004S1 on the B-G431B-ESC1 — the same values as in the simulation:

#include "sstep.h"

extern int board_pwm_write(void* ctx, const uint16_t compare[SSTEP_LEGS_MAX]);
extern int board_output_enable(void* ctx, bool enable);

const struct sstep_config motor_cfg = {
    .motor = {
        .r_mohm = 1600U,             /* 1.60 Ohm */
        .l_uh = 3000U,               /* 3.0 mH */
        .i_rated_ma = 2000U,
        .ke_uv_s_per_rad = 208600U,  /* Kt = 0.2086 V*s/rad: back-EMF feed-forward */
        .full_steps_per_rev = 200U,
    },
    .stage = {
        .topology = SSTEP_TOPOLOGY_SHARED_LEG,
        .vbus_nominal_mv = 24000U,
        .vbus_min_mv = 10000U,
        .vbus_max_mv = 30000U,
        .i_full_scale_ma = 4000U,    /* ADC full scale (placeholder: from the schematic) */
        .i_trip_ma = 3500U,
        .pwm_period_ticks = 4250U,   /* 170 MHz, centre-aligned, 20 kHz */
        .pwm_freq_hz = 20000U,
        .dead_time_ns = 133U,        /* effective dead time from ngspice */
        .adc_i_zero = 2048U,
        .adc_i_span = 2047,
        .adc_vbus_mv_full = 34320U,
        .adc_full = 4095U,
    },
    .ctrl = {
        .drive_mode = SSTEP_DRIVE_CURRENT,
        .fast_loop_hz = 20000U,
        .slow_loop_hz = 1000U,
        .microsteps = 16U,
        .current_bw_hz = 1000U,
        .i_run_ma = 2000U,
        .i_hold_ma = 1000U,
        .hold_delay_ms = 100U,
        .v_max = 16000U,             /* 5 rev/s */
        .accel = 160000U,            /* 50 rev/s^2 */
        .decel = 0U,                 /* same as accel */
    },
    .hal = {
        .context = NULL,
        .pwm_write = board_pwm_write,
        .output_enable = board_output_enable,
        .on_fault = NULL,
        .on_event = NULL,
    },
};

How to get each value:

Field How to obtain it r_mohm, l_uh datasheet, better measured (R with 4-wire, L at 1 kHz) ke_uv_s_per_rad back-EMF amplitude / speed of the spun motor (Motor Model); 0 disables the feed-forward vbus_* supply; vbus_min_mv < nominal < vbus_max_mv or 0 to disable a trip i_full_scale_ma, adc_i_zero, adc_i_span from the shunt, the amplifier gain and offset: span = I_full · R_shunt · G / V_ref · adc_full; negative adc_i_span for an inverting amplifier; measure the zero with the outputs off adc_vbus_mv_full, adc_full bus voltage divider: the bus voltage that gives the largest ADC reading pwm_period_ticks timer auto-reload of the centre-aligned PWM (compare for 100 %) dead_time_ns effective dead time (Power Stage Model); stored for a future compensation current_bw_hz 1 kHz is a good start at 20 kHz; at most fast_loop_hz / 4 v_max, accel microsteps per second (and per second²); with M = 16 one revolution is 3200 microsteps

Current measurement resolution

The simulation assumes a 4 A full scale (1.95 mA per ADC count). The current sense amplifiers of motor control boards are often designed for tens of amperes; compute the counts per ampere from the schematic before choosing the run current — a resolution coarser than about 1 % of the run current makes the current loop noisy.

sstep_init() checks every field and returns SSTEP_ERR_PARAM for a value out of range or a missing required callback, SSTEP_ERR_CONFIG for inconsistent values (for example i_run_ma above i_trip_ma or i_rated_ma, fast_loop_hz not a multiple of slow_loop_hz, current_bw_hz above fast_loop_hz / 4, a bus voltage trip on the wrong side of the nominal value) and SSTEP_ERR_UNSUPPORTED for a topology that is not compiled in.

docs.title: Connecting the loops to the hardware
docs.text:
The library expects:

  1. A centre-aligned PWM with one compare channel per leg. Compare 0 means the low side is on for the whole period, pwm_period_ticks the high side. Entries above the leg count of the topology are 0.
  2. Current sampling at the counter peak, the middle of the period where all low-side switches conduct: with low-side shunts the phase current flows through the shunt only then, and the sample equals the period average of the ripple.
  3. sstep_fast_loop() once per PWM period, right after the ADC conversion, with the raw counts of phase A, phase B and the bus voltage. The computed compare values are written by pwm_write() and take effect at the next timer update — the one-period delay the controller is designed for.
  4. sstep_slow_loop() at slow_loop_hz, from a timer task or the main loop, never concurrently with the commands (they run in the same context).
#include "sstep.h"

/* Board layer (your HAL): timer and ADC are configured elsewhere */
extern void timer_set_compare(uint32_t channel, uint16_t value);
extern void gate_driver_enable(bool enable);
extern uint16_t adc_read_injected(uint32_t rank);

static struct sstep drv;

static int pwm_write(void* ctx, const uint16_t compare[SSTEP_LEGS_MAX])
{
    (void)ctx;
    timer_set_compare(1U, compare[0]);   /* leg U: phase A+ */
    timer_set_compare(2U, compare[1]);   /* leg V: phase B+ */
    timer_set_compare(3U, compare[2]);   /* leg W: common   */
    return 0;
}

static int output_enable(void* ctx, bool enable)
{
    (void)ctx;
    gate_driver_enable(enable);          /* also: timer main output enable */
    return 0;
}

/* ADC end-of-conversion interrupt, triggered at the counter peak (20 kHz) */
void adc_injected_isr(void)
{
    const struct sstep_sample s = {
        .i_a = adc_read_injected(1U),
        .i_b = adc_read_injected(2U),
        .vbus = adc_read_injected(3U),
    };
    (void)sstep_fast_loop(&drv, &s);
}

/* 1 kHz timer task */
void control_task_1khz(void)
{
    (void)sstep_slow_loop(&drv);
}

int motor_start(struct sstep_config* cfg)
{
    cfg->hal.pwm_write = pwm_write;
    cfg->hal.output_enable = output_enable;
    int r = sstep_init(&drv, cfg);
    if (r == SSTEP_OK)
    {
        r = sstep_enable(&drv);
    }
    return r;
}

On the ESC1 the three legs are driven by the advanced timer TIM1 (one complementary channel per leg); phase A of the motor is connected between U and W, phase B between V and W. The exact channel assignment, the dead time register and the ADC trigger are documented with the port (P3).

docs.title: Commanding motion
docs.text:
#include "sstep.h"

static void on_event(void* ctx, enum sstep_event ev)
{
    (void)ctx;
    if (ev == SSTEP_EVENT_MOVE_DONE)
    {
        /* target reached: start the next move, signal the host... */
    }
}

void demo(struct sstep* m)
{
    struct sstep_status st;

    (void)sstep_set_position(m, 0);              /* homing: here is zero */
    (void)sstep_move_to(m, 6400);                /* two revolutions forward (M = 16) */
    (void)sstep_set_motion_limits(m, 32000U, 160000U, 0U);  /* from the next slow period */
    (void)sstep_run(m, -12800);                  /* turn backwards at 4 rev/s, smoothly */
    (void)sstep_stop(m);                         /* decelerate and hold */
    (void)sstep_get_status(m, &st);              /* state, position, currents, Vbus */
    (void)on_event;
}

Commands are accepted in HOLDING and MOVING; they return SSTEP_ERR_STATE when the driver is disabled or faulted. A new command replaces the running one without a velocity step. sstep_set_position() is only allowed at standstill and keeps the rotor where it is (only the numbering changes).

docs.title: Porting checklist
docs.text:
1. Measure R, L and the back-EMF constant of the motor; enter them.
  2. Compute the ADC scaling of the currents and of the bus voltage from the schematic; measure the current zero with the outputs disabled.
  3. Configure a centre-aligned PWM at pwm_freq_hz with the timer dead time; trigger the current ADC at the counter peak.
  4. Call sstep_fast_loop() from the ADC interrupt, sstep_slow_loop() at 1 kHz.
  5. Start with a current-limited supply, i_run_ma at half the rated current and a low v_max; check the phase currents with a current probe.
  6. Run the same configuration in the SIL diagram and compare.

docs.title: Motor Model
docs.text: The motor model is a two-phase hybrid stepper with sinusoidal back-EMF, a detent torque term, viscous and dry friction and a rigid load. It is written once (model/stepper_motor_f.sci) and used by the prototype, the Xcos plant block (in C) and the Python twins. This chapter gives the equations, the sign conventions, the parameters of the 17HS19-2004S1 and the limits of the model.

docs.title: State equations
docs.text:
The state is \(x = [\,i_A,\ i_B,\ \omega,\ \theta\,]\): the two phase currents (A), the mechanical speed (rad/s) and the mechanical rotor angle (rad). With \(p = N_s / 4\) electrical periods per mechanical turn (50 for a 200-step motor):

Electrical part

\[ \begin{aligned} L\,\frac{di_A}{dt} &= v_A - R\,i_A - e_A, \qquad e_A = -K_t\,\omega\,\sin(p\theta) \\ L\,\frac{di_B}{dt} &= v_B - R\,i_B - e_B, \qquad e_B = K_t\,\omega\,\cos(p\theta) \end{aligned} \]

Mechanical part

\[ \begin{aligned} J\,\frac{d\omega}{dt} &= T_e - T_L - T_f \\ \frac{d\theta}{dt} &= \omega \end{aligned} \]

Torques

\[ \begin{aligned} T_e &= K_t\,\left(-i_A \sin(p\theta) + i_B \cos(p\theta)\right) - T_d \sin(4p\theta) \\ T_f &= B\,\omega + T_c \tanh\left(\frac{\omega}{\omega_c}\right) \end{aligned} \] Symbol Meaning Unit \(v_A\), \(v_B\) phase voltages applied by the power stage V \(R\), \(L\) phase resistance and inductance (no mutual inductance between phases) Ω, H \(K_t\) torque constant = back-EMF constant N·m/A = V·s/rad \(T_d\) detent torque amplitude (period: one full step) N·m \(T_L\) load torque N·m \(B\) viscous friction N·m·s/rad \(T_c\), \(\omega_c\) dry (Coulomb) friction and its smoothing speed N·m, rad/s \(J\) rotor + load inertia kg·m²

The back-EMF and the torque come from the same flux linkage, so the electrical power \(e_A i_A + e_B i_B\) equals the mechanical power \(T_e\,\omega\) (without the detent term, which does no net work over a step). Test T00 checks this balance on 1000 random states (largest error 1.1·10⁻¹³ W).

docs.title: Sign convention
docs.text:
With the current vector

\[ i_A = I \cos\varphi, \qquad i_B = I \sin\varphi \]

the torque is \(T_e = K_t\,I \sin(\varphi - p\theta)\): it is zero and restoring at \(p\theta = \varphi\). The rotor therefore settles at \(p\theta = \varphi\), increasing \(\varphi\) turns it forward, and phase A leads phase B by 90°. The electrical angle between the field and the rotor, the load angle (electrical degrees),

\[ \delta = \varphi - p\theta \]

is the most useful quantity in every test: with a load \(T_L\) the rotor lags by \(\delta = \arcsin\left(T_L / (K_t I)\right)\), the largest static torque is \(K_t I\) at \(\delta = 90^\circ\), and beyond \(\delta \approx 180^\circ\) the rotor falls into the next pole — the motor has lost steps.

Note

An early project note used \(i_A = I \sin\varphi\), \(i_B = I \cos\varphi\). With the torque equation above that turns the rotor backwards; the library, the prototype and this manual all use the cosine/sine form.

docs.text:

The parameters are a Scilab structure returned by motor_17hs19_2004s1() (params/motor_17hs19_2004s1.sci); a test or a scenario changes a field (mot.Td = 0.02;) without touching the equations.

Measuring K_t

Spin the unpowered shaft (a drill), measure the open-circuit phase voltage amplitude \(E\) and the speed \(\omega\): \(K_t = E / \omega\). If the datasheet holding torque is meant for one phase only, K_t would be 0.295 N·m/A — 41 % more, which changes every speed limit in this manual.

The natural frequency is the stiffness of the "magnetic spring" \(p K_t I\) against the inertia; it decides the low-speed resonance (Results).

docs.title: Numerical solution
docs.text:
Use Solver Open-loop studies (stepper_simulate) Scilab ode (lsoda), rtol 10⁻⁸, atol 10⁻¹⁰ Closed loop, averaged power stage fixed-step RK4, 4 steps per PWM period (12.5 µs) Closed loop, switching power stage RK4 between the switching instants, at least 16 steps per period Python twin of the open-loop model scipy solve_ivp (Radau), rtol 10⁻¹⁰

The dry friction \(T_c \tanh(\omega/\omega_c)\) is stiff near zero speed (time constant \(J\omega_c / T_c\)). RK4 stays stable while \(h\,T_c / (J\omega_c) < 2.8\): with \(\omega_c\) = 0.05 rad/s and the 12.5 µs step of the closed loop that is \(T_c\) up to about 0.09 N·m. Increase \(\omega_c\) for larger friction values.

docs.title: Limits of the model
docs.text:
The model is meant for designing and testing the controller. It does not include:

  • magnetic saturation (inductance and K_t drop at high current);
  • harmonics of the back-EMF and of the torque other than the detent term;
  • mutual inductance between the phases;
  • temperature (R rises about 0.4 %/K in copper);
  • stiction (the dry friction is smoothed);
  • elasticity of the coupling and the load (one rigid inertia).

Effects that depend on these — the exact speed of the mid-band instability, the noise spectrum, the current at full saturation — must be checked on the hardware.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This manual describes the Stepper-C system: a control library for two-phase hybrid stepper motors written in C11, the Scilab/Xcos model it is developed and verified against, and the ngspice model of the power stage it will drive first. It is written for embedded engineers who want to use the library, check its behaviour in simulation, or extend the models. Every number in it was measured with the models and tests of the versions listed below.

docs.title: What the system is
docs.text:
Stepper-C replaces the closed "step/direction" driver chip with software: the microcontroller measures the two phase currents, runs a current controller per phase and writes the PWM of the power stage itself. The library computes everything between a motion command (move to position 3200) and the PWM compare values; the board code only reads the ADC and writes the timer.

Three repositories make up the system:

Repository Local folder Content Language / tool Stepper-C sfs-stepper-ctrl Stepper-C, the control library C11, CMake, GoogleTest sfs-stepper-sim sfs-stepper-sim Motor model, prototype of the control algorithms, software in the loop Scilab 2027, Xcos, Python twins sfs-stepper-power-spice sfs-stepper-power-spice Transistor-level model of one leg of the B-G431B-ESC1 power stage ngspice, Python

The library repository is published as Stepper-C; it is cloned into the folder sfs-stepper-ctrl, the name the simulation looks for.

The library is the product; the two models exist to find its limits before hardware does. The chain is closed in both directions: the C code runs unchanged inside Xcos, and the parameters the ngspice model extracts (effective dead time, leg resistance, diode drop) are written into the simulation.

docs.title: What it does and does not do
docs.text: Stepper-C does Why Closed-loop current control of both phases (PI with back-calculation anti-windup, back-EMF feed-forward) Microstepping torque follows the current, not the voltage; at speed only a current loop keeps the amplitude Microstepping 1 … 256 per full step from a 32-bit electrical angle Smooth motion, low noise; resolution independent of the step rate Trapezoidal motion profile with exact integer braking No overshoot, exact stop on the target, no velocity step when a move is replaced Two power stage topologies: two H-bridges, or three legs with a shared leg The shared-leg layout lets three-phase BLDC boards (B-G431B-ESC1) drive a stepper Bus voltage compensation and voltage vector limiting with the direction kept Torque direction is preserved when the bridge runs out of voltage Overcurrent, over- and undervoltage trips; external faults Protects the board in the fast loop, within one PWM period Fixed point (Q15/Q31) or float arithmetic, chosen at build time Runs on MCUs with and without FPU Stepper-C does not Why / what to use instead Generate step/direction pulses for an external driver chip It is the driver; use the chip's own interface for that case Read the clock, sleep or allocate memory Time comes from the configured loop rates; the instance is allocated by the application Configure timers, ADC or GPIO Board-specific; done by the application through the callbacks Close a position loop on an encoder (yet) Open-loop microstepping; the load angle is visible in simulation (planned extension) Compensate the dead time (yet) The configuration field exists; the ngspice results define the value (planned)

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
• Firmware engineers integrating stepper control on an STM32, a Cortex-M0 or any MCU with two ADC channels and a PWM timer: read Stepper-C Library and the API Reference.
  • Control and system engineers who want to know where the drive loses steps, resonates or saturates: read Motor Model, Control Algorithms and Results.
  • Hardware engineers choosing dead time, gate resistors and shunt sampling: read Power Stage Model.
  • Students who want to open one file, press Start and see a stepper motor being controlled by real embedded C code: read Software in the Loop.

Models are not hardware

The results in this manual come from models with datasheet parameters and several stated assumptions (detent torque, dry friction, gate resistors, dead time). They show where to look and what to expect. Check every limit on the real motor and board before relying on it, and start with a current-limited supply.

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text: Full step 1.8° for a 200-step motor: one quarter of an electrical period. Microstep A fraction 1/M of a full step; M = 16 gives 3200 positions per revolution. Fast loop The code that runs every PWM period: current measurement, PI controllers, voltage limit, PWM write. Slow loop The code that runs at 1 kHz: motion profile, current amplitude, events. Shared leg A power stage with three half-bridges where phase A is connected between legs U and W and phase B between V and W; W is common to both phases. Software in the loop (SIL) The real library code, compiled for the PC, running inside the Xcos simulation against the motor model. Twin A second implementation of the same algorithm in another language (Scilab ↔ Python, Scilab ↔ C) used to cross-check results sample by sample.

docs.title: Power Stage Model
docs.text: sfs-stepper-power-spice models one half-bridge leg of the B-G431B-ESC1 in ngspice: the L6387E gate driver, two STL180N6F7 MOSFETs, gate resistors, the bootstrap supply and the low-side current shunt. It answers the questions an averaged model cannot: how long the transistors really take to switch, how much of the timer dead time is left, what the phase voltage loses in the dead time, and when the shunt voltage is valid for sampling. The results are exported to the simulation.

docs.title: The leg circuit
docs.text:
File Content models/stl180n6f7_sfs.lib STL180N6F7 as an ngspice VDMOS model, fitted by this project to the datasheet models/l6387_behav.lib L6387E behavioural model circuits/esc1_leg.lib subcircuit ESC1_LEG: driver, MOSFETs, gate resistors, bootstrap capacitor, shunt, layout inductances tools/run_tests.py test benches SP01–SP03, fit, export tools/plot_leg.py switch node waveforms (docs/leg_edges.png)

The test bench drives the leg with the timer signals of the simulation: a centre-aligned period from counter peak to counter peak, the high side commanded on in \(\left[\frac{T_s}{2}(1 - d),\ \frac{T_s}{2}(1 + d)\right]\), every turn-on delayed by the timer dead time. The phase is a constant current source (the 3 mH phase inductance keeps the current almost constant within 50 µs). Six periods are simulated and the last one is evaluated.

docs.title: Device models
docs.text:
STL180N6F7 (VDMOS). The ST SPICE model is not part of the repository (its licence is ST's). The project model uses the ngspice VDMOS device — smooth, with a body diode and a non-linear gate-drain capacitance — fitted to the datasheet values:

Quantity Model (SP01) Datasheet (typical) Rds(on), VGS 10 V, 16 A, 25 °C 1.903 mΩ 1.9 mΩ Rds(on) at 100 °C 2.466 mΩ (×1.30) — Body diode VSD at 32 A 0.997 V ≤ 1.2 V (max) Body diode at 2 A 0.727 V — Ciss at VDS 25 V 4801 pF 4825 pF Coss at VDS 25 V 2189 pF 2240 pF Crss at VDS 25 V 207 pF 216 pF Qg, VGS 0 … 10 V, 30 V, 32 A 78.3 nC 79.5 nC

Assumptions: VGS(th) 3.0 V, internal gate resistance 1.2 Ω, diode 0.70 V at 1 A and 1.0 V at 32 A, transit time 2 ns. The switching times of the datasheet (td(on) 33.9 ns, tr 35.6 ns, td(off) 68.9 ns, tf 42.2 ns) are measured with a stronger gate drive and are not used as fit targets.

L6387E (behavioural). Interlocking (HIN and LIN both high → both outputs low; the L6387E inserts no dead time of its own), a propagation delay of 107 ns (mean of ton 110 ns and toff 105 ns), output stages with 30 Ω source and 18 Ω sink resistance (from the 400 mA / 650 mA short-circuit currents), and the bootstrap DMOS (125 Ω) with its diode. The logic edges are smoothed and delayed with matched lossless lines, so no XSPICE is needed.

docs.title: Board values and assumptions
docs.text:
The ESC1 user manual does not list the passive values of the power stage. Until they are read from the schematic (MB1419), the model uses:

Value Assumed Influence Timer dead time 500 ns the main input; set in the firmware Gate driver supply 12 V gate drive strength Gate resistors 10 Ω, no turn-off diode turn-off delay, Miller bump Bootstrap capacitor 1 µF high-side gate voltage Shunt 3 mΩ, 1 nH leg resistance, shunt settling Commutation loop 3 nH, damped by 1 Ω across each inductance ringing

They are the BOARD dictionary at the top of tools/run_tests.py; change them there and rerun.

docs.title: What happens in the dead time
docs.text:
The figure shows the switch node at both edges for +2 A (current out of the leg) and −2 A:

  • The high side turns on 700 ns after the ideal edge for +2 A: 500 ns timer dead time
  • 107 ns driver delay + the time to charge the gate to the Miller plateau. Until then the low-side diode holds the node at −0.73 V.
  • For −2 A the node rises already in the dead time: the low side switches off and the phase current itself charges the switch node to the bus (soft switching).
  • The high side turns off slowly: the gate discharges through 18 Ω + 10 Ω + 1.2 Ω from 11 V to the Miller plateau and stays there while the drain voltage changes — about 400 ns. The switch node falls 571 ns after the ideal edge for +2 A.

As a result most of the 500 ns timer dead time is consumed by the turn-off of the other transistor:

Result Value Meaning Gap between the driven gates (both below VGS(th) 3 V) 154 ns margin of the dead time; reducing the timer dead time below about 350 ns risks shoot-through Effective dead time of the phase voltage (1–3 A) 133 ns what the step model of the simulation and a future compensation must use Gate of the off switch while the other turns on up to 3.73 V Cgd·dv/dt against the gate resistor: above VGS(th), a short cross conduction at every edge with the assumed 10 Ω

docs.title: Dead time voltage error
docs.text:
The mean leg voltage over a period differs from the ideal \(d\,V_{\mathrm{bus}}\). The simulation uses the step model

\[ \Delta v_{\mathrm{leg}} = -\operatorname{sign}(i)\,\left(V_{\mathrm{bus}} + 2V_d\right)\frac{t_{d,\mathrm{eff}}}{T_s} - R_{\mathrm{leg}}\,i \]

with \(t_{d,\mathrm{eff}}\) fitted for 1 A ≤ \(|i|\) ≤ 3 A (largest deviation 12.8 mV) and \(R_{\mathrm{leg}} = (R_{ds} + R_{ds} + R_{\mathrm{shunt}}) / 2\) = 3.4 mΩ. Below 1 A the real error is smaller: the phase current charges the switch node capacitance (about 2 × Coss) too slowly to finish the swing within the dead time — 50 % of the step model at 0.5 A, about 25 % at 0.25 A. The measured table (leg_error_table) is exported for a better compensation later.

docs.text:
Case Shunt at the sampling instant Ideal \(-i\,R_{\mathrm{sh}}\) Settled (2 %) after the low-side timer edge d = 0.5, +2 A −6.000 mV −6.000 mV 345 ns d = 0.5, −2 A +6.000 mV +6.000 mV 344 ns d = 0.9, +2 A −6.000 mV −6.000 mV 345 ns

The low-side shunt carries the phase current also in the dead time (through the body diode of the low switch), so the shunt voltage is valid from 345 ns after the low-side command. With an ADC sampling time of 250 ns before the centre, a centred sample stays valid up to a leg duty of 0.956. With the shared leg at full voltage the largest leg duty approaches 1; the library does not limit it yet (planned).

docs.title: Results and Design Guidance
docs.text: This chapter collects what the models say about the 17HS19-2004S1 on the B-G431B-ESC1 at 24 V, and turns it into guidance for configuring the library and the board. All values come from the tests in the Test Catalogue; the assumptions behind them (datasheet motor parameters, detent and friction values, board passives) are listed in Motor Model and Power Stage Model.

docs.title: Current loop
docs.text:
Quantity Value Test Bandwidth (design) 1 kHz — Step 0 → 2 A: overshoot / rise (90 %) / settling (2 %) 1.12 % / 0.35 ms / 0.40 ms T04 Same with R ×0.9 … 1.3, L ×0.8 … 1.2 overshoot ≤ 5.2 %, settling ≤ 1.6 ms T08 Phase lag at 1 rev/s about 4° T03, T05 Current ripple at 2 A, locked (20 kHz, 3 mH) 23 mA p-p T10

The pole-zero cancellation keeps the loop well damped for the whole tolerance range of the datasheet; a hot winding (R +30 %) with a low inductance slows the last 2 % of the step to 1.6 ms but does not destabilise it. Guidance: 1 kHz bandwidth at 20 kHz PWM is a safe default; do not exceed fast_loop_hz / 4 (enforced by sstep_init()).

docs.text:
Speed Two H-bridges: current, scale, load angle Shared leg (ESC1): current, scale, load angle 2 rev/s 2.00 A, 1.00, 6° 2.00 A, 1.00, 6° 4 rev/s 1.97 A, 1.00, 12° 1.97 A, 1.00, 12° 6 rev/s 1.93 A, 1.00, 18° 1.90 A, 0.81, 19–20° 8 rev/s 1.86 A, 0.97, 24° 1.56 A, 0.51, 36–39° 9 rev/s 1.73 A, 0.83, 31° 1.27 A, 0.46, 48–50° 10 rev/s 1.46 A, 0.71, 42° 1.02 A, 0.41, 51–63° (oscillating) 12 rev/s limit cycle, 16–95° limit cycle, 3–134°

(Unloaded rotor, 2 A reference, back-EMF feed-forward on; scale is the smallest factor the power stage applied to the requested voltage, 1 = not limited.)

With three legs the largest circular voltage is Vbus/√2: the ESC1 reaches the voltage limit at about 6 rev/s at 24 V, two H-bridges at about 8 rev/s. Beyond the limit the current — and the torque — drops with speed, and the load angle grows even without load.

Guidance: at 24 V on the ESC1 plan for at most 8 rev/s with useful torque reserve; the torque available at speed n is roughly K_t · I(n), minus the angle already used for acceleration. A higher bus voltage moves every speed in the table up proportionally (the ESC1 accepts up to 6S LiPo voltages).

docs.title: Rotor resonance
docs.text:
Low-speed resonance. The rotor on the current vector is a spring-mass system with f_n = √(p K_t I / J) / 2π = 254 Hz at 2 A (248 Hz with the current loop). Any torque ripple at that frequency excites it. The detent torque has four periods per electrical period, so it excites the rotor at 4 p n = f_n, i.e. about 1.25 rev/s with the rotor alone: with an assumed detent torque of 0.02 N·m the oscillation reaches ±14° there against ±3–5° elsewhere. A load inertia lowers f_n (∝ 1/√J) and with it the resonant speed.

Mid-band instability. As long as the current loop controls the current, it damps the rotor: no oscillation at 5 rev/s. Once the bridge limits the voltage, the drive behaves like a voltage source and the back-EMF coupling undamps the rotor: ±1.3° at 8 rev/s, a limit cycle of ±48° at 11 rev/s on the ESC1 (from about 12 rev/s with two H-bridges).

Guidance:

  • Do not run continuously at the low-speed resonance; accelerate through it. Microstepping (M ≥ 16) already removes the full-step excitation; the detent torque remains.
  • Keep the operating speed below the voltage limit (previous section) — that is also the region where the rotor is damped.
  • Measure f_n on the real motor (a small angle step, as in T11a) and the detent torque; the resonant speed depends on both.
  • Active damping in the library (from the back-EMF estimate) is a possible extension.

docs.title: Software in the Loop
docs.text: The software-in-the-loop (SIL) diagram runs the real C code of Stepper-C — the same sources that go into the firmware — against the motor model in Xcos. It is the place where a user without Scilab knowledge sees the library control a motor: open one file, press Start, watch currents, speed, load angle and position. It is also a test bench: S01–S04 compare it sample by sample with the Scilab prototype.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
1. Install Scilab 2027 and, on Windows, Visual Studio 2022 or the free Build Tools with the workload Desktop development with C++.
  2. Clone Stepper-C into the folder sfs-stepper-ctrl next to sfs-stepper-sim (or set the environment variable SSTEP_CTRL_DIR to it).
  3. Open start_sil.sce in Scilab and press F5.
  4. Xcos opens xcos/stepper_sil.zcos. Press Start (▶).

The default scenario moves the motor two revolutions (6400 microsteps at 1/16) with 5 rev/s and 50 rev/s² on the B-G431B-ESC1 at 24 V. The scope shows four plots: the phase currents with their references, the speed in rpm, the load angle in electrical degrees (above 90° the motor is close to losing steps) and the commanded and real rotor positions in microsteps.

Variable Values Effect sil_backend "FIXED" (default), "FLOAT" numeric backend of the compiled library; switching needs a Scilab restart sil_regenerate %f (default), %t %t builds the diagram again from xcos/sil_diagram.sci (needed after a change of the block interfaces)

docs.title: The diagram
docs.text:
Block Computational function (C, type 4) Inputs → outputs Parameters SampleCLK Xcos → event every Ts = 1/fs Ts STEPPER_CTRL sstep_xcos_ctrl ADC [i_a i_b vbus] (counts) → [compare(4) enabled], monitor [φ position velocity state faults iA* iB*] sil_ctrl_rpar(mot, brd, ctl, mp, cmds) STEPPER_PLANT sstep_xcos_plant [compare(4) enabled] → ADC sample, [iA iB ω θ vA vB |iA|max |iB|max] sil_plant_rpar(mot, brd, loads, locked, 4) STEPPER_MONITOR sstep_xcos_monitor plant + controller monitor → currents, rpm, load angle, positions, 12 values for the workspace [mot.Ns, mp.M] CMSCOPE Xcos 4 plots ranges from the context TOWS_c Xcos → workspace variable sil buffer N_log END_c Xcos stops at T_end T_end

What the controller block does. At initialisation it builds a struct sstep_config from the parameter vector, calls sstep_init() (a configuration error stops the simulation with the library's status text) and sstep_enable(). On every clock event it applies the commands whose time has come, calls sstep_slow_loop() every ratio events, converts the ADC input to a struct sstep_sample, calls sstep_fast_loop() and outputs the compare values the library wrote through its pwm_write callback.

What the plant block does. It integrates the motor over one PWM period with the leg voltages of the previous period (the one-period computation delay of the MCU), using the averaged or the switching power stage (brd.stage), applies the load torque steps, and models the ADC: counts = round(zero + i / i_full · span), clamped to 0 … adc_full, and the bus voltage reading.

docs.title: Build and rebuild
docs.text:
sil_build(backend, force) copies the library sources and sil/c/sstep_xcos.c into sil/build/<backend>/, compiles them with the compiler Scilab finds (tbx_build_src; Visual Studio on Windows, gcc on Linux) with -DSSTEP_CFG_MATH_BACKEND=…, and links the shared library. The build happens once; it is repeated automatically when any source file differs from its copy in the build folder. sil/build/ is ignored by Git.

The library is searched in this order: SSTEP_CTRL_DIR, the submodule ext/sfs-stepper-ctrl, the sibling folder ../sfs-stepper-ctrl.

docs.title: Closed-loop prototype
docs.text:
sim_closed_loop is the discrete prototype of the Stepper-C fast loop, run period by period exactly in the order of the MCU: sample the currents, compute the references and the controller, apply the voltage computed in the previous period (c.delay = 1) for one period, integrate the motor.

[rec, st, ext] = sim_closed_loop(mot, brd, c, ref, refp, T, locked, st)
Argument Meaning mot, brd, c motor, board, controller; c.mot (optional) is the motor the controller is tuned for, if different from the plant ref, refp, st reference function [r, st] = ref(t, refp, st) returning [I; φ; ω_ref; T_L], its parameters and state T simulated time [s] locked %t: rotor locked (current loop tests) rec one row per period: t iA iB w θ iA_ref iB_ref vA vB k I φ (k = power stage scale, 1 = not limited) ext one row per period: iA_min iA_max iB_min iB_max vA_mean vB_mean (switching stage: within the period)

Reference functions:

Function Reference ref_current_step constant angle, current step I0 → I1 at t_step ref_const_speed constant current, constant electrical frequency ref_speed_ramp constant current, speed ramp to rev_s in t_ramp, optional load TL ref_angle_step constant current, angle step 0 → φ1 (rotor natural frequency) ref_motion the motion generator: commands [t kind value] (see below)

Example — current step on a locked rotor, the test T04:

mot = motor_17hs19_2004s1(); brd = board_bg431b_esc1(); c = ctrl_default();
refp = struct("I0", 0, "I1", 2, "t_step", 1e-3, "phi", 0);
rec = sim_closed_loop(mot, brd, c, ref_current_step, refp, 6e-3, %t);
plot(rec(:, 1), rec(:, 2), rec(:, 1), rec(:, 6));     // iA and its reference

docs.title: Motion generator twin
docs.text:
motion_init, motion_slow and motion_step reproduce the integer motion generator of Stepper-C bit for bit (model/sim_int.sci provides C-style integer division and square root). ref_motion turns it into a reference: it calls the slow loop every ratio fast periods and interpolates the angle exactly like the library.

Command [t kind value] Meaning kind 1 MOVE move to value microsteps kind 2 RUN run at value microsteps/s kind 3 STOP decelerate to standstill kind 4 LOAD load torque value N·m from time t (simulation only) 
mp = motion_default();
st = motion_init(mot, brd, mp, [0, 1, 6400]);          // move 2 revolutions at t = 0
[rec, st] = sim_closed_loop(mot, brd, c, ref_motion, [], 0.6, %f, st);
// st.hist: [t pos v vel_q16 mode] per slow period

The figure shows the test T05: the rotor follows the commanded speed with a load angle of 15° at 50 rev/s² (inertia of the rotor only), the run current drops to the hold current 100 ms after the move, and the move ends exactly on 6400 microsteps after 499 ms.

docs.title: Power stage models
docs.text:
brd.stage Model Use "avg" (default) each leg delivers duty · Vbus (bridge_avg) fast; all control tests "switching" bridge_switching.sci: centre-aligned legs, turn-on delayed by the dead time, body diode in the dead time (−Vd or Vbus + Vd by current direction), Rds(on); RK4 between the switching instants (stepper_period_sw) ripple, peak current, dead time distortion; about 5× slower

The period starts at the counter peak (all low sides on, the sampling instant); the high side of a leg with duty d is commanded on in [Ts/2 (1 − d), Ts/2 (1 + d)]. A pulse shorter than the dead time disappears. With all outputs disabled every leg is in the dead state (only the diodes conduct).

With ideal switches the switching model gives the same sampled currents as the averaged model within 0.01 mA (test T10). The dead time changes the mean phase voltage by −2 sign(i) (Vbus + 2 Vd) td / Ts; the stage values come from ngspice (stage_esc1_spice(): effective dead time 133 ns, leg resistance 3.4 mΩ, diode 0.73 V).

brd.stage = "switching";
sp = struct("I", 2, "rev_s", 4, "t_ramp", 0.05, "Ns", mot.Ns);
[rec, st, ext] = sim_closed_loop(mot, brd, c, ref_speed_ramp, sp, 0.15);
peak = max(abs(ext(:, 1:4)));                   // largest current including the ripple

demos/demo_switching.sce plots the sampled current with its ripple band, the ripple per period and the dead time voltage error.

docs.title: Python twins
docs.text:
Every Scilab algorithm has a Python twin in tools/. The twins are independent implementations used to cross-check the Scilab code (tests X01–X04), to prototype tests quickly and to generate the reference CSV files.

Twin Covers Run ref_model.py motor model (scipy Radau), T00–T02, X01 reference python tools/ref_model.py [--write] ref_ctrl.py averaged stage, PI loop, B01, T03, T04, X02 reference python tools/ref_ctrl.py [--write] ref_motion.py integer motion generator (bit-exact with C), T05–T07, T09, X03 reference python tools/ref_motion.py [--write] ref_switching.py switching stage, T10, X04 reference python tools/ref_switching.py [--write] ref_ext.py T08, T11, T12 python tools/ref_ext.py

--write regenerates the reference files in tests/reference/. Requirements: numpy, scipy.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
exec("tests/run_all.sce", -1);

The runner executes every test script with error catching, prints PASS/FAIL lines with the measured values and a failure count, and exits with status 1 in batch mode (scilab-cli -f tests/run_all.sce) when a test fails. Test variables use the prefix rt_ so that test scripts cannot overwrite them. The complete list with the pass criteria is in the Test Catalogue.

docs.title: Adapting the model to another motor or board
docs.text:
1. Copy params/motor_17hs19_2004s1.sci to a new function with the values of your motor (R, L, I_rated, Kt, Ns, J), or change the fields in a script.
  2. Copy params/board_bg431b_esc1.sci for another board: bus voltage, topology ("full" or "shared"), PWM frequency and period, trip levels, ADC scaling.
  3. Run T01–T04 first (electrical model and current loop), then the motion tests.
  4. For the switching stage, set dead_ns, rds_on, vd from your power stage (or adapt the ngspice model and export).

docs.title: System Architecture
docs.text: This chapter shows how the library, the simulation and the power stage model fit together, which data flows between them, and the development workflow that keeps them consistent. The individual modules are described in their own chapters.

docs.title: The three repositories
docs.text:
Part Role in the system Gives to the others Takes from the others Stepper-C (GitHub, folder sfs-stepper-ctrl) The product: control loops for the MCU C sources compiled into the Xcos blocks Algorithms first proven in the prototype; dead time value for compensation Simulation (sfs-stepper-sim) Motor model, prototype of every algorithm, SIL test bench Reference results, limits (speed, resonance, robustness) The library sources (SIL); the switching stage parameters from ngspice Power stage model (sfs-stepper-power-spice) Transistor-level view of one ESC1 leg params/stage_esc1_spice.sci / .json: effective dead time, leg resistance, diode drop Board values (gate resistors, shunt, dead time) Hardware (B-G431B-ESC1 + 17HS19-2004S1) The target of the first port (P3) Measured R, L, Kt, dead time, gate waveforms The library and its configuration

The repositories are independent Git repositories that sit next to each other:

sfs-stepper/
├── sfs-stepper-ctrl/          Stepper-C library
├── sfs-stepper-sim/           Scilab/Xcos model, SIL, Python twins
├── sfs-stepper-power-spice/   ngspice model of the power stage
└── sfs-stepper-article/       this manual (website + PDF), repository Stepper-C-Motor-Control-Library

The simulation finds the library through the environment variable SSTEP_CTRL_DIR, a Git submodule ext/sfs-stepper-ctrl, or the sibling folder ../sfs-stepper-ctrl (in that order). The ngspice runner writes its export into ../sfs-stepper-sim/params/ when that folder exists.

docs.title: Signal chain
docs.text:
From a command to a turning shaft:

  1. The application calls sstep_move_to() (or sstep_run(), sstep_stop()).
  2. Every slow loop period (1 ms) the motion generator advances the position with the acceleration and velocity limits, chooses the current amplitude (run or hold) and publishes a setpoint: the electrical angle at the start of the period, its increment per fast period, the current amplitude and the back-EMF feed-forward.
  3. Every fast loop period (50 µs at 20 kHz) sstep_fast_loop() converts the ADC counts to currents, checks the trip levels, computes the current references I cos φ, I sin φ, runs one PI controller per phase, adds the feed-forward, limits and maps the voltage vector to the legs of the topology and calls pwm_write().
  4. The power stage applies the leg voltages; the motor turns the phase currents into torque; the ADC samples the currents at the centre of the next PWM period.

The same chain exists three times — in C (the library), in Scilab (the prototype) and in Python (the twin) — and the three are compared sample by sample.

docs.title: Development workflow
docs.text:
The work follows the order of the figure, and each step is checked against the previous one before the next starts:

  1. Model. The motor equations are written once (stepper_motor_f) and checked against analytic results (T00–T02) and an independent Python solver (X01).
  2. Prototype. Each control algorithm is first written in Scilab and tested on the model (T03–T12).
  3. Library. The algorithm is implemented in C11 for both numeric backends, with unit tests and 100 % coverage.
  4. Software in the loop. The C code runs in Xcos against the same model; S01–S04 must match the prototype.
  5. Power stage. ngspice extracts the switching parameters of the real board; the simulation uses them.
  6. Hardware. The library is ported to the B-G431B-ESC1; measured motor and board values flow back into the models.

Rule: the prototype follows the library

The Scilab prototype always implements the current algorithm of the library. A change in Stepper-C is ported to the prototype and to its Python twin in the same step, so that the SIL comparison compares identical algorithms.
